title: I Posted the Sitar-Mizrab Hours After They Camped My Numbered Gourd

parts.text: I stepped into the raga room at 6:07 p.m. and mentor Farah was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE SITAR. NINETY MINUTES. MIZRABS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was twenty-nine, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered mizrabs. Farah shrugged. "Mentors are the gourd." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover wires on my numbered gourd. Then I asked for the mizrab log. At 6:15 the desk pinged why Farah's name was on my wires. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Farah's leftover wires on my numbered gourd.

social.video_title: They camped my numbered sitar gourd on my hours — Part 1/2
social.description: Raga room, leftover wires, a ninety-minute clock she posted. I logged the mizrabs. Would you have asked for the mizrab log?

parts.text: Farah called it sympathetic tune-up until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the wire still. The gourd went back to my numbered slot. Farah ran a slot of her own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS ARE NOT THE GOURD. I keep my mizrabs in a labeled tin. Farah brown-bags her tune-ups. The raga room finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Mentors are not the gourd — Part 2/2
social.description: Mizrab log, numbered gourd, and a second line on the board. Was a sympathetic tune-up ever my wires?
